content: The content provided outlines various cervical cancer screening strategies, their effectiveness, and associated outcomes. Below is a professional summary of the key points: 1. Screening Algorithms and Stakeholders: Multiple cervical cancer screening algorithms were evaluated, including primary HPV screening, cytology-based screening, and combinations of HPV testing with genotyping or visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) for triage. These strategies involve collaboration among national and regional health authorities, professional societies, hospital-level providers, primary care providers, community health workers, and the community itself. 2. Effectiveness of Screening Strategies: Primary HPV screening without triage, conducted every five years for women aged 30–50, was the most effective strategy, reducing cervical cancer incidence by 57%. HPV screening with 16/18 genotyping for triage achieved a 56% reduction in incidence. Other HPV-based strategies, regardless of triage options, consistently reduced cervical cancer incidence by over 50%. VIA-based screening required more frequent intervals (e.g., every three years) to achieve comparable reductions in incidence. 3. Benefits vs. Harms: HPV-based screening strategies required fewer precancer treatment events compared to VIA-based strategies. HPV genotyping (16/18) for triage was similarly effective to HPV screening without triage but resulted in fewer precancer treatments. HPV-based strategies also led to fewer adverse obstetric outcomes, such as preterm deliveries, compared to VIA-based approaches. 4. Patient Preferences and Acceptability: Many women expressed willingness to travel long distances for screening, particularly for VIA-based programs. Factors influencing screening participation included urban residency, health insurance, prior knowledge of cervical cancer, and positive attitudes toward screening. Barriers included logistical challenges, lack of access to modern cancer therapies, and geographic constraints. 5. Special Populations (WLHIV): Women living with HIV (WLHIV) benefited significantly from more frequent screening starting at younger ages. Primary HPV screening every three years for ages 25–50 reduced cervical cancer incidence by 70%. The benefits of screening in this high-burden population were larger in magnitude compared to the general population, but the associated harms were also greater. 6. Cost-Effectiveness: Primary HPV screening without triage was the most cost-effective approach, particularly when conducted at 10-year intervals for women aged 35–45. HPV screening with 16/18 genotyping for triage had similar cost-effectiveness outcomes and offered a better balance of benefits to harms. VIA-based strategies were less cost-effective due to the need for more frequent screening and higher treatment burdens. 7. Resource Utilization: HPV-based strategies required fewer biopsies and precancer treatment events compared to VIA-based approaches. Logistical issues, such as maintaining a consistent supply of cryotherapy gas, posed challenges for VIA-based treatment delivery. 8. Conclusion: For women in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs), primary HPV screening without triage and HPV screening with 16/18 genotyping at five-year intervals for ages 30–50 were the most effective and cost-efficient strategies. These approaches balanced benefits and harms better than other screening methods. For WLHIV, more frequent HPV screening starting at younger ages was highly effective in reducing cervical cancer incidence. This analysis highlights the importance of tailoring cervical cancer screening strategies to population needs, resource availability, and healthcare infrastructure.
